reasons: Gaia RV shows the star has a stellar-mass companion: gaia_rv_variable True from gaia_rv_nb_transits 22.0, gaia_rv_chisq_pvalue 0.0, gaia_rv_renormalised_gof 71.17, gaia_rv_epoch_scatter_km_s 24.6, gaia_rv_amplitude_robust_km_s 76.9. A scatter of tens of km/s cannot come from a planet. Step 9 bounds the companion at this period by gaia_rv_semi_amplitude_upper_limit_km_s 34.8 and gaia_rv_companion_mass_upper_limit_solar_masses 0.533, so an M-dwarf companion at 11.53 d is fully allowed by the RV. gaia_ruwe 1.48 (caution 'RUWE above 1.4') is consistent with the same companion.

The light curve cannot show the companion is planet-sized. The step 9 fit is grazing: fit_impact_parameter 1.179 +/- 0.1704, fit_radius_ratio 0.2317 +/- 0.15824, planet_radius_earth_radii 35.98 +/- 24.57, with the caution 'transit fit not converged in 100000 steps'. The verification record shows the fit alternating between a non-grazing solution (b 0.45-0.48, Rp ~5 Earth radii, density ratio 19.9-21.7 in runs 9674c6b and c651077, i.e. the step 7 caution 'duration does not fit the star', fitted_to_expected_scaled_semi_major_axis 3.66, duration_hours 1.44) and a grazing solution (b 1.18, Rp 36, stellar_density_fit_to_tic_ratio 0.645 in runs a0cf3d7 and 7983853). Both solutions say the same thing: a short, shallow (fit_depth_ppm 1460) dip on a stellar_radius_solar_radii 1.4258 star at 11.53 d that is either grazing or too short for the star. A grazing M dwarf at a/R 13.83 (fit_scaled_semi_major_axis) reproduces this naturally; combined with the RV, a grazing eclipsing binary is the most likely explanation.

I partly disagree with the mechanical reasoning. 'radius 36.0 Earth radii is above 22.4' is not decisive on its own because the grazing geometry leaves the radius almost unconstrained (error 24.57 Earth radii). The drop rests on the Gaia RV scatter together with the grazing/short-duration geometry, not on the nominal radius. The conclusion is the same.

TRICERATOPS does not support a planet despite its label: fpp_mean 0.4075 +/- 0.021 is far above any validation threshold. nfpp_mean 0 and nearby_scenarios_excluded True only remove the neighbours (gaia_neighbours_able_to_cause_dip: Gaia DR3 3288837740527400576 at 23" G 17.7 needs 63%; Gaia DR3 3288834789885910784 at 51" G 16.6 needs 23%), so the remaining ~41% probability is in on-target companion scenarios, which is what the RV indicates. The 'neighbour able to cause dip' caution is itself addressed by the pixel check: pixel_verdict 'on target', S98 SNR 6.3, best star TIC 450075592, and the difference image puts the dip squarely on the target pixel.

The secondary eclipse is marginal but points in the binary direction: secondary_depth_ppm 166 +/- 63 (2.6 sigma) against secondary_maximum_planet_depth_ppm 287; not a refutation, but no support for a planet. ellipsoidal_amplitude_ppm -41 +/- 79 is uninformative at this separation and cannot exclude a 0.5 solar-mass companion. odd_even_difference_sigma 0.33 shows the 11.53 d period is correct, so the dip is a real eclipse of TIC 450075592, not a false alarm or blend.

Sector 5 adds nothing and I give the 'depths differ between sectors' caution no weight: other_sector_results 'S5 TESS-SPOC: SNR 4.0, expected SNR 8.6', joint_search_snr 12.9 equals the S98 BLS SNR 12.9, and the step 9 figure shows the only S5 data lying at -32 to -24 h from mid-transit, i.e. no transit is actually covered. The cutout_sector_depth_consistency_p_value 2.55e-12 (S5 r2.0 -113 +/- 140 vs S98 r2.0 1205 +/- 125) reflects ephemeris propagation over ~217 cycles with fit_period_error_days 0.00118741, not a genuine depth change.

Not 'held': released_tess_sectors_not_in_all_sector_verification is empty, and unreleased_tess_sectors_observing_the_star '110' would add photometry but would not remove the Gaia RV evidence of a stellar-mass companion; only ground-based RVs could, which are outside this pipeline. exofop_tois, exofop_ctois and published_signal are all empty so the signal is new, but the evidence makes it most likely a grazing eclipsing binary rather than a planet.
